unit.title: Perform manual heating, and thermal cutting

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before heating or cutting, what must you find out from the drawing or job sheet?
options: The colour of paint to be used on the job once it is finished
The type and thickness of the metal, and the shape and size needed
The name of the gas supplier and the date of the last cylinder delivery
How long the same job took the last trainee who did it at the Centre

questions.stem: Why should oil, grease and thick paint be removed from steel before heating or cutting?
options: Oil and paint make the steel harder once it has cooled down
Clean steel needs a carburising flame instead of the usual neutral flame
Paint stops the regulator gauges from giving a true reading
They burn and give off fumes, and they spoil the heat or the cut

questions.stem: How do you choose the size of cutting nozzle and the gas pressures for a job?
options: From the maker's chart, by the type and thickness of the metal
By using the biggest nozzle so the cut is always fast
By setting both gases to the same high pressure
By copying the settings left on the outfit by the last person

questions.stem: Which eye protection should you wear when oxy-acetylene cutting steel up to about 25 mm thick?
options: Clear safety glasses only, because there is no arc to protect against
An arc welding helmet with a very dark shade 13 filter fitted
Gas welding goggles or a face shield with about a shade 3–5 filter
Dark sunglasses with good plastic lenses that block the glare

questions.stem: Which clothing is best for heating and cutting work?
options: Long-sleeved flame-resistant cotton or leather, with no turn-ups or open pockets
A nylon or polyester jacket, because hot sparks bounce off the smooth shiny cloth
Shorts and a T-shirt, so the body keeps cool near the hot flame
Old overalls soaked in oil, because the oil keeps the sparks off

questions.stem: Sparks and slag from cutting can travel a long way. How far around the work should anything that can burn be cleared or covered?
options: Up to half a metre
About 2 metres
About 4 metres
10 metres or more

questions.stem: Why should someone keep watching the area for some time after hot work has finished?
options: The gas left in the hoses may cool down and start to leak out
A hidden spark can smoulder for a while and start a fire later
The cut pieces may change shape as they cool over an hour
The regulators must be watched until their needles stop moving

questions.stem: What is the main danger when heating or cutting galvanised (zinc-coated) steel?
options: The zinc coating makes the steel explode as soon as it reaches red heat
The zinc coating makes the preheat flame blow out often
Zinc fumes, which can cause metal fume fever if breathed in
The zinc turns the cutting oxygen into a poisonous gas

questions.stem: A steel drum that held fuel has to be cut in half. What should be done?
options: Do not cut it until a competent person has cleaned it and made it safe
Cut it quickly, before the fumes inside have time to build up
Fill it with pure oxygen first, so that any fumes left inside burn off cleanly
Cut it with the cap screwed on tight so the fumes stay inside it

questions.stem: Why should you not let cutting sparks and slag fall straight onto a concrete floor?
options: The concrete takes in the oxygen and the cut stops halfway
The heat can make the concrete crack and burst (spall)
The slag sticks to the concrete and stains it a red colour
Concrete carries electricity back up to the cutting torch

questions.stem: Why must acetylene cylinders always be stored and used standing upright?
options: So that the cylinder can cool down faster in the hot Jamaican sun
So that the regulator gauges on top give a true reading
So that the gas comes out at a higher and steadier pressure
So that the acetone inside cannot come out through the valve

questions.stem: Acetylene becomes unstable at high pressure. What is the highest working pressure it should be used at?
options: About 100 kPa (15 psi)
About 400 kPa (60 psi)
About 700 kPa (100 psi)
About 1400 kPa (200 psi)

questions.stem: Why must oil and grease never be put on oxygen fittings or regulators?
options: Oil makes the thread seals too tight to undo later
Oil mixes with oxygen to make more acetylene gas
Oil can burst into flame by itself in pure oxygen
Oil blocks the filter inside the flashback arrestor

questions.stem: LPG (propane) is sometimes used as the fuel gas for heating. If it leaks, where does it collect?
options: High up under the roof, because it is lighter than air
Low down in pits and drains, because it is heavier than air
Around the flame, because the flame pulls the gas towards it
Nowhere, because it mixes into the air and disappears at once

questions.stem: How can you tell fuel gas hose fittings from oxygen fittings?
options: Fuel gas nuts have right-hand threads, the same as oxygen nuts
Fuel gas nuts are bigger and are always made of hard steel
Fuel gas nuts are always wrapped with tape to seal them
Fuel gas nuts have left-hand threads and are often notched

questions.stem: What does a flashback arrestor do?
options: It lowers the cylinder pressure to a working pressure
It shows how much gas is left inside the cylinder
It stops a flame travelling back to the regulator and cylinder
It mixes the oxygen and the fuel gas together in just the right amounts

questions.stem: Before you open a cylinder valve, what should you do with the regulator?
options: Wind the adjusting screw out until it is loose, and stand to one side
Wind the adjusting screw fully in, so that gas flows out at once
Take the glass off the gauge so that you can see the needle clearly
Put your face close to the gauge so you can read it as it rises

questions.stem: How far should the acetylene cylinder valve be opened?
options: Fully open, so that the gas flow is never held back
At least three full turns, and then the key removed and put away safely
Fully open, then the key taken away and kept in the store
Less than one and a half turns, with the key left on the valve

questions.stem: How should you check the hoses and fittings for gas leaks?
options: Hold a small flame close to each joint and watch for it to flare
Brush on leak-detection solution and look for bubbles
Close the cylinder valves, then smell each joint closely
Squeeze the hoses hard and feel for any soft places

questions.stem: On an oxy-acetylene cutting nozzle, what comes out of the centre hole when the cutting lever is pressed?
options: Acetylene, to make the flame hotter
Mixed gas, to make all the preheat flames bigger
Pure oxygen, to burn and blow out the steel
Compressed air, to blow the sparks away

questions.stem: How should a dirty or blocked cutting nozzle be cleaned?
options: With tip cleaners of the right size, pushed straight in and out
With a drill bit a little bigger than the hole, to open it up
By tapping it hard on the steel bench until the dirt falls out
By pushing a nail or a piece of wire firmly into each hole

questions.stem: Why are the hoses purged (each gas let through briefly) before the torch is lit?
options: To warm the gas up so that it lights more easily
To check that both regulators are reading correctly
To blow dust off the work before the cut starts
To clear out any air or mixed gas left in the hoses

questions.stem: When lighting an oxy-acetylene torch, which torch valve is opened first?
options: The oxygen valve, a little, before the gas is lit
The acetylene valve, a little, before it is lit
Both valves together, fully open, before lighting
The oxygen valve, fully open, then the acetylene

questions.stem: What does a neutral oxy-acetylene flame look like?
options: A long white feather of gas around the inner cone
A short, pointed inner cone that hisses loudly
A clear, sharp, rounded inner cone with no feather
A yellow, smoky flame with no inner cone at all

questions.stem: What is a backfire?
options: A loud pop as the flame goes into the nozzle, then goes out or relights
Hot slag from the cut blowing back up towards the operator's face and chest
Black smoke coming off the flame when acetylene is first lit
The regulator needle jumping back to zero when the valve opens

questions.stem: While cutting, you hear a squeal or hiss inside the torch and the handle gets hot. What should you do?
options: Turn the oxygen up higher to blow the flame back out
Dip the torch in water and then carry on cutting
Unscrew the nozzle to let the trapped gas escape
Close the torch valves and the cylinder valves at once

questions.stem: Which job is a normal use of manual heating with an oxy-fuel torch?
options: Heating a full gas cylinder so the gas flows out faster
Preheating thick steel before welding, to reduce cracking
Hardening mild steel by heating it and leaving it in the air
Drying welding electrodes in their box with the flame

questions.stem: A nut has rusted onto a bolt. How does heating the nut help to free it?
options: The heat makes the bolt shrink a little, away from the nut
The heat welds the rust into a softer metal
The nut expands with the heat and loosens on the bolt
The heat melts the threads so they slide apart

questions.stem: A flat bar has a bow (curve) in it. Where should the heat go to straighten it?
options: On the outside (long side) of the curve
On the inside (short side) of the curve
Evenly along the whole length of the bar
At the two ends of the bar only

questions.stem: Why does a heated spot on steel pull the steel towards it as it cools?
options: The hot spot gets lighter, so the rest of the bar slowly falls towards it
The flame pushes the soft metal into its new shape while hot
The cold metal around the spot expands and fills the space
The hot spot is held by cold metal, thickens, then shrinks on cooling

questions.stem: When flame straightening mild steel, how hot should each heated spot get?
options: Bright yellow, nearly white
Hot enough to start melting
No hotter than a dull red
Just warm to the touch

questions.stem: When hot bending a steel bar held in a vice, where should the heat be put?
options: On one small spot on the inside of the bend only
Evenly all round the bar, over the length of the bend
On the part of the bar held inside the vice jaws
Along the full length of the bar, from end to end

questions.stem: How does oxy-fuel cutting cut through steel?
options: The steel is heated red hot, then an oxygen jet burns it and blows it out
The flame melts the steel, and the melted metal drips out of the cut
The oxygen jet cools the steel very quickly so that it cracks along the line
The fuel gas eats into the steel like an acid and removes it

questions.stem: Which metal can be cut well with a normal oxy-fuel cutting torch?
options: Aluminium sheet
Stainless steel plate
Copper or brass bar
Mild steel plate

questions.stem: When cutting with oxy-acetylene, how far should the tips of the preheat inner cones be from the plate?
options: Pressed down firmly onto the plate surface
About 2–3 mm, just clear of the surface
About 25 mm above the plate surface
About 50 mm above the plate surface

questions.stem: Why should you cut along the waste side of the marked line?
options: So that the sparks fly away from your body
So that the marked line is easier to see through your dark goggles
So that the width of the cut does not make the part too small
So that the cut goes faster and uses less gas

questions.stem: When starting a cut at the edge of a plate, when do you press the cutting oxygen lever?
options: When the edge of the plate glows bright red
As soon as the flame touches the plate
When the edge has melted and begun to drip
Before the preheat flames have been lit

questions.stem: What does a good oxy-fuel cut look like?
options: A rounded top edge with beads of melted steel along it
Deep gouges in the face and lots of slag stuck underneath
Drag lines that curve far back from the direction of travel
A sharp square top edge, fine straight drag lines, little slag

questions.stem: The drag lines curve far back and the cut does not go right through. What is the most likely cause?
options: Travel speed too slow
Travel speed too fast
Preheat flame too hot
Nozzle held too close

questions.stem: The top edge of a cut is melted and rounded over. What is a likely cause?
options: The travel speed was much too fast
The plate was cleaned before cutting
The preheat flame was too strong or too close
The fuel gas hose was much longer than the usual one

questions.stem: A flame-cut edge is to be welded. How should it be cleaned first?
options: Chip off the slag and grind off the oxide to bright metal
Paint it with oil so that the weld flows more easily
Leave the oxide layer on, because it acts like a flux for welding
Wash it with water and weld it while it is still wet

questions.stem: What is one advantage of plasma cutting over oxy-fuel cutting?
options: It needs no electricity, so it can be used anywhere
It needs no eye protection at all, because there is no flame
It works best on wood, plastic and other non-metals
It can cut stainless steel and aluminium as well as steel

questions.stem: Before changing the nozzle (tip) or electrode on a plasma torch, what must you do?
options: Turn the air pressure up to cool the torch down
Switch off and isolate the power at the machine
Hold the trigger in so the torch stays cool
Take the earth clamp off the job, and nothing more

questions.stem: Why must the plasma cutter's work (earth) clamp be fixed firmly to clean metal on the job?
options: To hold the job still so it cannot slide about on the table
To keep the torch cool during a long cut
To complete the circuit so the cutting arc can form
To measure the thickness of the metal being cut

questions.stem: At the end of the day, how do you shut down an oxy-acetylene outfit?
options: Close cylinder valves, bleed the lines, release regulator screws, close torch valves
Close the torch valves only, and leave the gas in the hoses for tomorrow
Take the regulators off first, while the cylinder valves are still open
Close the cylinder valves, and leave the regulator screws wound fully in

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What colour is the hose for the fuel gas (acetylene or LPG)?
What tool should be used to light an oxy-fuel torch?
What do we call the crayon-like stick that melts at a set temperature, used to show that a part is hot enough?
What is the name for the slot, or the width of metal removed, made by a cut?
What document lists the hazards of a job and how each one will be controlled?
What is the name of the flame that has more acetylene than oxygen and shows a white feather?
In plasma cutting, what is the name of the small arc made inside the torch before the cutting arc jumps to the work?
What written permission is often needed before heating or cutting outside the workshop, such as on a site?
What small valve, fitted where each hose joins the torch, lets the gas flow one way only?
What shape of heat is usually marked on the edge area of a bent bar or plate for flame straightening?
What is the name for starting a cut by burning a hole through the middle of a plate, away from the edge?
What is the name of the large nozzle with many flame holes, used to heat a wide area?
Most small plasma cutters use one gas, supplied by a compressor. Which gas is it?
What is screwed on or fitted over a cylinder valve to protect it while the cylinder is being moved?
On a regulator, what is the name of the gauge that shows the pressure inside the cylinder?

essays.stem: Describe the personal protective equipment (PPE) needed for oxy-fuel heating and cutting, and say what each item protects against.
essays.modelAnswer: Gas welding goggles or a face shield with a filter of about shade 3–5 for cutting, or as the maker's chart says, protect the eyes from glare, heat and flying sparks. For plasma cutting the shade is chosen from the chart for the current used. Leather gauntlet gloves protect the hands from heat, hot metal and sparks. Long-sleeved flame-resistant cotton or leather clothing, buttoned up, with no turn-ups or open pockets, stops sparks from catching in the clothes and burning the skin. Nylon and polyester must not be worn because they melt onto the skin. A leather apron and sleeves give extra cover when cutting. Safety boots protect the feet from falling plate and hot slag, with the trousers worn over the boots. A cap protects the hair. Ear protection is needed for plasma cutting and grinding, and a respirator where fumes cannot be kept away, for example from coated steel.
markingPoints: Goggles or face shield with a suitable shade (about 3–5 for cutting; from the chart for plasma) — glare, heat and sparks
Leather gauntlet gloves — heat, hot metal and sparks
Long-sleeved flame-resistant cotton or leather clothing, no turn-ups, no nylon — burns from sparks
Safety boots with trousers over them — falling metal and hot slag
Extra items as needed: apron, cap, ear protection, respirator for coated steel

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to set up an oxy-acetylene outfit from the cylinders to the torch, ready for lighting.
essays.modelAnswer: Chain both cylinders upright on the trolley. Check that the valve outlets and regulator threads are clean, undamaged and free of oil. Fit the oxygen regulator (right-hand thread) and the acetylene regulator (left-hand thread) and tighten them with the correct spanner. Fit a flashback arrestor to each regulator outlet. Check the hoses for cuts, burns and cracks, then connect them the right way round, with the red hose on the fuel gas side and check valves where the hoses join the torch. Fit the right nozzle for the job from the maker's chart. Wind out both regulator adjusting screws, stand to one side and open the cylinder valves slowly, the acetylene valve less than one and a half turns with the key left on. Set the working pressures from the chart, keeping acetylene below about 100 kPa (15 psi). Leak-test every joint with leak-detection solution, then purge each hose in turn in a well-ventilated place.
markingPoints: Cylinders secured upright; fittings checked clean, undamaged and free of oil
Regulators fitted (fuel gas left-hand thread), flashback arrestors at the regulators and check valves at the torch
Hoses checked and connected the right way round; correct nozzle fitted from the chart
Adjusting screws released, stand aside, cylinder valves opened slowly (acetylene under 1½ turns, key left on); pressures set from the chart
Every joint leak-tested with solution, and each hose purged before lighting

essays.stem: Explain how to light an oxy-acetylene cutting torch and set the preheat flame, and how to check that the cutting oxygen is set correctly.
essays.modelAnswer: First check the set-up, the pressures and the area, and put on full PPE. Point the torch away from people, hoses and cylinders. Open the acetylene torch valve a little and light the gas with a spark lighter, never a match or a cigarette lighter. Open the acetylene a little more until the flame stops giving off black smoke. Then slowly open the preheat oxygen valve. At first the flame has a long white feather (a carburising flame). Keep adding oxygen until the feather just disappears into a clear, sharp, rounded inner cone at each preheat hole. This is a neutral flame. Now press the cutting oxygen lever. The preheat flames may show a small feather again, so adjust the preheat oxygen to make them neutral with the lever held down. The cutting oxygen stream should be long, straight and clean. If the flame keeps popping or will not stay neutral, shut down and check the nozzle and the pressures.
markingPoints: Checks first; torch pointed away from people, hoses and cylinders
Acetylene opened a little first and lit with a spark lighter; smoke cleared
Oxygen added until the feather goes — sharp, rounded inner cones (neutral)
Preheat reset to neutral with the cutting oxygen lever held down
Cutting stream straight and clean; shut down and check if it pops or will not stay neutral

essays.stem: Explain how oxy-fuel cutting works, and why it cuts mild steel well but will not cut aluminium or stainless steel properly.
essays.modelAnswer: Oxy-fuel cutting is a burning process, not a melting process. The preheat flames heat a small spot of steel to its ignition (kindling) temperature, when it glows bright red. A jet of pure oxygen is then turned on. The hot iron burns quickly in the oxygen and turns into iron oxide, and the force of the jet blows the liquid oxide out of the cut, leaving a narrow slot called the kerf. The heat from the burning helps to keep the cut going as the torch moves along. This only works when the metal burns before it melts, and when its oxide melts at a lower temperature than the metal so that it can be blown away. Mild steel meets these conditions. Aluminium melts before it burns, and its oxide melts at a much higher temperature than the metal. Stainless steel forms a chromium oxide skin that will not melt and flow away. These metals are cut with a plasma cutter instead.
markingPoints: Preheat flames raise the steel to ignition temperature (bright red)
Pure oxygen jet burns (oxidises) the iron and blows the oxide out of the kerf
Conditions: the metal must burn before it melts, and its oxide must melt below the metal and flow
Aluminium melts first and has a high-melting oxide; stainless steel forms a chromium oxide that will not flow
Plasma cutting is used for these metals

essays.stem: Describe what a good oxy-fuel cut looks like. Then name two faults in a cut, and give the cause and the cure for each.
essays.modelAnswer: A good cut has a sharp, square top edge, a smooth face with fine drag lines that are nearly straight up and down, a square bottom edge and only a little slag that knocks off easily. The cut is on the line and the part is the right size. Fault 1: drag lines that curve far back, a rough face and a cut that may not go right through. The cause is travelling too fast, or too little cutting oxygen. The cure is to slow down and check the oxygen pressure against the maker's chart. Fault 2: a melted, rounded top edge with beads of steel along it. The cause is a preheat flame that is too strong, a nozzle held too close, or travel that is too slow. The cure is to turn the preheat down, keep the inner cones about 2–3 mm above the plate and travel at a steady speed. Heavy slag stuck to the bottom is another fault, often from going too slowly or a dirty nozzle.
markingPoints: Good cut: square sharp top edge, fine near-vertical drag lines, little slag, on size
Fault 1 named with a correct cause (for example too fast — curved drag lines, cut not through)
A correct cure for fault 1
Fault 2 named with a correct cause (for example rounded top edge — preheat too strong, too close or too slow)
A correct cure for fault 2

essays.stem: Explain how to straighten a flat bar that has been bent along its width (bowed edgeways) by flame heating, and why the method works.
essays.modelAnswer: Lay the bar on a flat bench and use a straight edge to find the bow. Mark the outside (long) edge of the curve at its highest point. On the flat face, mark a V shape (a wedge) with its wide end at the outside edge and its point about two-thirds of the way across the bar. Set a neutral flame with a heating nozzle. Heat the V, starting at the point and working out towards the wide end, until the steel is a dull red right through. Do not go hotter than dull red. Let the bar cool in still air, then check it with the straight edge. If it is still bowed, make another V-heat beside the first one, not on top of it. The method works because the heated metal tries to expand but is held by the cold metal around it, so it is squeezed and gets thicker. When it cools it shrinks and is now shorter, which pulls the outside edge in and straightens the bar. Handle the bar with tongs and mark it HOT.
markingPoints: Find and mark the bow with a straight edge; heat goes on the outside (long) side
V or wedge heat with the wide end at the outside edge, heated from the point outwards
Heat only to dull red; cool in still air, check, and add heats beside the first if needed
Why: the heated metal is held by cold metal, thickens, then shrinks on cooling and pulls the bar straight
Safe handling: tongs, PPE, hot metal marked

essays.stem: Describe how to heat and bend a 40 mm × 10 mm mild steel flat bar to 90° in a vice, safely and accurately.
essays.modelAnswer: Read the drawing and mark the bend line with soapstone. Set the bar in a heavy vice that is bolted down, with the bend line just above the jaws. Clear anything that can burn and have an extinguisher ready. Fit a heating nozzle or a large welding nozzle and set a neutral flame. Heat evenly over the whole bend area, a little wider than the bar thickness, moving the flame across both faces and both edges so that the heat goes right through, until the steel is bright red. Pull the bar over steadily with a bending bar or tap it over with a heavy hammer, keeping the bend at the line. Check the angle with a square while the bar is still in the vice. If it needs more bending, reheat it rather than forcing cold steel, which can crack. Let the bar cool slowly in air. Use tongs and gloves to handle it, and mark it HOT until it is cool.
markingPoints: Bend line marked; bar held firmly in a strong vice at the line
Fire precautions and a suitable nozzle with a neutral flame
Heat evenly through the whole bend area to bright red, not on one spot
Bend steadily at the line and check 90° with a square; reheat rather than force cold steel
Cool in air; handle with tongs and mark HOT

essays.stem: Compare plasma cutting with oxy-fuel cutting. Give two advantages of each, and the main safety points for plasma cutting.
essays.modelAnswer: Plasma cutting uses an electric arc forced through a small nozzle with compressed air, making a very hot jet that melts the metal and blows it away. Advantages of plasma: it cuts any metal that conducts electricity, including stainless steel and aluminium; and it is fast on thin metal, with a narrow cut and little heat, so there is less distortion. Oxy-fuel cutting burns the steel in a jet of oxygen. Advantages of oxy-fuel: it needs no electricity, so it can be used anywhere on site; and it cuts thick steel well with cheaper equipment. The same outfit can also be used for heating and bending. Safety for plasma: the machine uses a high voltage, so check the cables, keep everything dry, fix the work clamp to clean metal, and switch off and isolate before changing the nozzle or electrode. Wear a filter shade from the maker's chart, gloves, flame-resistant clothing and ear protection. Keep good ventilation, because the arc makes fumes, and clear anything that can burn.
markingPoints: Plasma advantages: cuts stainless steel, aluminium and other conducting metals; fast with a narrow cut and less distortion on thin metal
Oxy-fuel advantages: no electricity needed, good on thick steel, cheaper, also used for heating
Plasma electrical safety: check cables, keep dry, isolate before changing consumables
Plasma PPE: shade from the maker's chart, gloves, clothing, ear protection
Ventilation for fumes and fire precautions

essays.stem: Explain how to prevent fires when heating or cutting in the workshop or on site, before, during and after the job.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the job, do a risk assessment and get a hot work permit if the work is outside the hot work bay. Move anything that can burn at least 10 m away, or cover it with fire blankets, and check behind walls, under floors and in gaps where sparks can fall. Never cut drums or tanks that held fuel unless a competent person has made them safe. Have a suitable extinguisher ready and know where the alarm and the way out are. Leak-test the equipment. During the job, keep the hoses away from sparks and hot metal, and point the flame away from cylinders and people. Have a fire watcher where sparks may go out of sight. Never leave a lit torch on the bench. After the job, shut the gas off, cool or mark the hot metal and check the whole area. The fire watcher stays for a set time after the work stops, often 30 to 60 minutes as the permit says, because hidden sparks can smoulder.
markingPoints: Before: risk assessment and permit; combustibles removed or covered (about 10 m); hidden gaps checked
Containers that held fuel never cut unless made safe by a competent person
Extinguisher ready; alarm and exit known; equipment leak-tested
During: hoses and cylinders kept from sparks; flame pointed safely; fire watcher posted
After: gas off, hot metal marked, area watched for a set time for smouldering

essays.stem: Describe how to shut down an oxy-acetylene outfit at the end of the day, store the equipment, and report any faults you found.
essays.modelAnswer: Put the flame out at the torch in the way the maker's instructions say. Close both cylinder valves. Open the oxygen torch valve to let the gas in the oxygen hose and regulator escape, then close it, and do the same for the acetylene, one gas at a time, in a ventilated place away from flames. Check that the gauges read zero. Wind out the regulator adjusting screws until they are loose, and close the torch valves. Coil the hoses neatly and hang them off the floor, away from oil, heat and sharp edges. Leave the cylinders chained upright, and fit the valve caps if the regulators are taken off. Put the torch and nozzles away clean. Cool or mark any hot metal, sweep up the slag and check the area for smouldering sparks. Report any fault, such as a leaking fitting, a damaged hose, a gauge that sticks or a nozzle that keeps popping, to the instructor. Tag the item out of use and write it in the equipment log.
markingPoints: Flame put out at the torch; both cylinder valves closed
Each line bled one gas at a time; gauges at zero; adjusting screws released; torch valves closed
Hoses coiled and stored off the floor away from oil and heat; cylinders left chained, caps fitted when needed
Area cleaned, hot metal marked, checked for smouldering sparks
Faults reported to the instructor, item tagged out of use and logged

practical1.title: Set up an oxy-acetylene outfit, heat-bend a flat bar to 90° and flame-straighten a bowed bar
practical1.brief: As a group, with the instructor present, set up an oxy-acetylene outfit at the hot work bay: check the cylinders, fit the regulators, flashback arrestors, hoses and check valves, and leak-test every joint with leak-detection solution. Every member then lights the torch with a heating nozzle, sets a neutral flame, and heats and bends one piece of 40 mm × 10 mm mild steel flat bar (300 mm long) to 90° at a marked line in the vice. Next, the group flame-straightens one bowed bar: every member makes at least one V-heat while the assessor watches, and the group checks the bar with a straight edge between heats. Finish by shutting the outfit down correctly and cleaning the area. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Oxy-acetylene outfit with regulators, flashback arrestors, hoses and torch check valves
Heating nozzle (multi-flame) or large welding nozzle, and a spark lighter
Leak-detection solution and a small brush
One piece of 40 mm × 10 mm mild steel flat bar, 300 mm long, for each member
One bowed mild steel flat bar, about 1 m long, for straightening
Heavy bench vice, engineer's square, steel rule, straight edge and soapstone
Tongs, a fire extinguisher and a fire blanket
photos: The outfit set up, with every member in full PPE
The leak test: solution on the regulator and hose joints
A member's neutral flame (close-up of the inner cone)
A bar heated at the bend line in the vice
Each member's finished 90° bend checked with a square
The bowed bar with the V-heats marked, and again after straightening, against a straight edge
The outfit shut down and the area cleaned
checklist: Wore the correct PPE throughout, including goggles with a suitable shade
Checked the cylinders, regulators, hoses and safety devices before use, and took part in the leak test
Lit the torch in the right order and set a neutral flame
Heated the bend area evenly to bright red and bent the bar to 90° (within about 2°) at the line
Placed the V-heat on the outside of the bow and kept the heat to dull red
Handled hot metal with tongs and marked it HOT
Shut down the outfit correctly: cylinders closed, lines bled, screws released
Left the work area safe and tidy
safety: Cylinders chained upright; acetylene used below about 100 kPa (15 psi); follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Remove or cover anything that can burn; keep an extinguisher at hand
Never point the flame at people, hoses or cylinders; hang the torch up when it is not in use
Treat all bars as hot: use tongs, mark them HOT and let them cool in a safe place

practical2.title: Straight-line oxy-fuel cutting of strips from 10 mm plate, and a plasma cut on thin sheet
practical2.brief: As a group, mark out and cut strips from 10 mm mild steel plate with an oxy-acetylene cutting torch. Every member cuts two strips 40 mm wide and 300 mm long: one freehand along a soapstone line and one using a clamped straight-edge guide. Every member also makes a 300 mm straight cut in 3 mm mild steel sheet with the plasma cutter, using a guide. Each member removes the slag and measures their strips, and the group compares the cut faces (drag lines, top edge, slag) and writes the faults found on a card beside the pieces. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the cutting is finished and the area is clean.
materials: Oxy-acetylene cutting outfit with flashback arrestors and check valves
Cutting nozzle to suit 10 mm plate (from the maker's chart), tip cleaners and a spark lighter
10 mm mild steel plate, about 600 mm × 300 mm
3 mm mild steel sheet, about 300 mm × 300 mm
Plasma cutter with a clean, dry compressed-air supply
Steel straight edge or angle-iron guide, and G-clamps
Steel rule, tape, square, soapstone, chipping hammer and wire brush
Cutting table with a slag tray, tongs and a fire extinguisher
photos: The plate marked out with 40 mm strips
Preheating at the plate edge before the cut
A guided cut in progress, with the member in full PPE
Each member's two strips, cut faces turned up, with name labels
The plasma cutter set up, with the work clamp on clean metal
The plasma-cut sheet, with the group's fault card beside the pieces
The cutting table and area cleaned, with the gases turned off
checklist: Wore the correct PPE, with a suitable filter shade for oxy-fuel and for plasma cutting
Checked the outfit and leak-tested it before lighting
Set a neutral preheat flame and held the inner cones about 2–3 mm above the plate
Started the cut at bright red and kept a steady speed along the line
Freehand and guided strips are 40 mm wide within about 2 mm, with square edges and little slag
Fixed the plasma work clamp to clean metal and switched off before touching the torch parts
Removed the slag and correctly named one fault and its cause on their pieces
Shut down the equipment and left the area safe and clean
safety: Cut only over the cutting table with a slag tray, never onto concrete
Clear or cover anything that can burn for at least 10 m; keep an extinguisher at hand
Watch where the cut-off piece will fall; keep feet and hoses clear
Isolate the plasma cutter before changing consumables; keep its cables dry and undamaged
Make sure there is good ventilation; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
